chapter.title: Objects and Arrays in State
chapter.description: Why you must replace state instead of mutating it, and the patterns for doing so.

blocks.text: React decides whether to re-render by comparing the new state with the old one by reference. Mutating an object keeps the same reference, so React sees no change and skips the update.
Array patterns
`push`, `pop`, `splice`, `sort` and `reverse` all mutate in place. Copy first with a spread, or use `map`, `filter`, `concat` and `slice`, which return new arrays.
Object patterns
Deeply nested state is a signal to flatten your data or to move it into a reducer. If you find yourself spreading three levels deep, restructure instead.
Keep state minimal
Do not store anything you can calculate from something else. Derived values in state go stale; derived values computed during render never do.

blocks.text: Calling the setter does not change the variable you are holding. It schedules an update. The current render keeps the value it started with.
This is not a bug. `count` is a `const` belonging to this render. The next render gets a fresh `count` with the new value.
Batching
React batches every state update triggered in the same event into one re-render. Three setter calls do not cause three renders.
All three calls read the same `count` from the current render, so all three schedule 'set it to 1'.
The updater function
When the next value depends on the previous one, pass a function. React calls it with the latest pending value, so the calls stack correctly.
Rule of thumb: if the new value is computed from the old one, use the updater form. It is always safe, and it avoids a whole class of stale value bugs.
Lazy initial state
The argument to `useState` is evaluated on every render even though it is only used once. If computing it is expensive, pass a function instead and React calls it only on the first render.

blocks.text: Two sibling components cannot see each other's state. When both need the same value, move it up to their closest common parent. This is called **lifting state up**.

blocks.caption: One source of truth in the parent, two children kept in sync.

blocks.text: Where should a piece of state live?

items: Find every component that reads the value.
Put the state there, and pass the value and an updater down.

blocks.text: If the common parent is many levels up, you are hitting prop drilling. Context or a state library solves that, and both are covered in the intermediate track.
